claim: Fecal microbiota density varies across mammalian species with a 216-fold difference between the median of the most dense and least dense gut microbiota.
source: we observed significant differences in microbiota density across the mammalian species (H = 69.0, p = 6.72 x 10−9; Kruskal-Wallis) with a 216-fold difference between the median of the most dense and least dense gut microbiota (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) of experimental measurements across mammalian species, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At the taxonomic rank of order, there are significant differences in microbiota density among mammals.
source: At the higher taxonomic rank of order, where we sampled at least two unique species (Atriodactyla, Carnivora, Primates, and Rodentia), we still found significant differences in microbiota density (H = 39.0, p = 3.39 x 10−9; Kruskal-Wallis), suggesting that evolutionarily conserved host features impact microbiota density.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) of experimental data grouped by taxonomic order.

claim: Evolutionarily conserved host features impact microbiota density.
source: At the higher taxonomic rank of order, where we sampled at least two unique species (Atriodactyla, Carnivora, Primates, and Rodentia), we still found significant differences in microbiota density (H = 39.0, p = 3.39 x 10−9; Kruskal-Wallis), suggesting that evolutionarily conserved host features impact microbiota density.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that microbiota density differs significantly at the order level, suggesting phylogenetically conserved traits influence density.

claim: There is no correlation between microbiota density and fecal water content in mammals.
source: We found no correlation between microbiota density and either fecal water content (ρ = -0.0418, p = 0.892, Spearman; Figure 1B) or host size (mass) (ρ = -0.364, p = 0.167, Spearman; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing no significant relationship between microbiota density and fecal water content.

claim: There is no correlation between microbiota density and host size (mass) in mammals.
source: We found no correlation between microbiota density and either fecal water content (ρ = -0.0418, p = 0.892, Spearman; Figure 1B) or host size (mass) (ρ = -0.364, p = 0.167, Spearman; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing no significant relationship between microbiota density and host mass.

claim: Animals from order Carnivora have significantly reduced microbiota densities compared with other mammals studied.
source: Nonetheless, animals from order Carnivora (dog, ferret, lion, red panda, and tiger), with simple gut architectures adapted to carnivorous diets, had significantly reduced microbiota densities compared with the rest of the mammals studied (p = 6.14 x 10−10, Mann-Whitney, Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) comparing Carnivora to other mammalian orders.

claim: Animals from order Carnivora have simple gut architectures adapted to carnivorous diets.
source: Nonetheless, animals from order Carnivora (dog, ferret, lion, red panda, and tiger), with simple gut architectures adapted to carnivorous diets, had significantly reduced microbiota densities compared with the rest of the mammals studied (p = 6.14 x 10−10, Mann-Whitney, Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about the anatomical features of Carnivora digestive systems.

claim: The lion and red panda microbiotas reached higher microbiota densities in mice than in their native hosts.
source: In germ-free Swiss Webster mice colonized with four of the lowest density microbiotas in our initial screen (lion, elephant, ferret, and red panda), the lion and red panda microbiotas reached higher microbiota densities in the mouse than in the native host (Figure 1D), suggesting their densities were limited by the carrying capacity of their host (which could include factors like intestinal architecture, host diet and host social behaviors).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing microbiota density in native hosts versus gnotobiotic mice.

claim: The densities of lion and red panda microbiotas in their native hosts were limited by the carrying capacity of their host.
source: In germ-free Swiss Webster mice colonized with four of the lowest density microbiotas in our initial screen (lion, elephant, ferret, and red panda), the lion and red panda microbiotas reached higher microbiota densities in the mouse than in the native host (Figure 1D), suggesting their densities were limited by the carrying capacity of their host (which could include factors like intestinal architecture, host diet and host social behaviors).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that these microbiotas reached higher densities in mice, suggesting host factors limited their density in native hosts.

claim: The elephant and ferret microbiotas colonized mice at densities comparable to those in the native host and significantly less dense than a mouse microbiota.
source: The elephant and ferret microbiotas colonized mice at densities comparable to those in the native host and significantly less dense than a mouse microbiota (Figure 1D), suggesting their densities are limited by the fitness of each microbiota that cannot reach the mouse carrying capacity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing microbiota densities across conditions.

claim: The densities of elephant and ferret microbiotas are limited by the fitness of each microbiota that cannot reach the mouse carrying capacity.
source: The elephant and ferret microbiotas colonized mice at densities comparable to those in the native host and significantly less dense than a mouse microbiota (Figure 1D), suggesting their densities are limited by the fitness of each microbiota that cannot reach the mouse carrying capacity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that these microbiotas did not reach mouse-level densities even in the mouse host.

claim: Microbiota density represents the combined influence of host carrying capacity and community fitness.
source: Altogether, these mammalian microbiota samples and germ-free transfer experiments demonstrate that as in macroecology, microbiota density represents the combined influence of host carrying capacity and community fitness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the gnotobiotic experiments showing both host and microbial factors influence density.

claim: Only 9 of the 14 tested antibiotics significantly decreased gut microbiota density compared to untreated animals.
source: Only 9 of the 14 tested antibiotics significantly decreased gut microbiota density compared to untreated animals (p < 0.05 for each; Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction), and the taxa reduced by each antibiotic were not strongly reflective of the antibiotic's spectrum (see Supplemental Results and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from antibiotic treatment experiments.

claim: The taxa reduced by each antibiotic were not strongly reflective of the antibiotic's spectrum.
source: Only 9 of the 14 tested antibiotics significantly decreased gut microbiota density compared to untreated animals (p < 0.05 for each; Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction), and the taxa reduced by each antibiotic were not strongly reflective of the antibiotic's spectrum (see Supplemental Results and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data showing antibiotic effects on specific taxa.

claim: There were substantial differences in each density-reducing antibiotic's depleting capacity.
source: Amongst these 9 density-reducing antibiotics, there were substantial differences in each drug's depleting capacity (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A comparing antibiotic effects.

claim: PEG 3350 reduced microbiota density.
source: Of the laxatives, PEG 3350 reduced microbiota density (p = 2.22 x 10−4), while lactulose increased it (p = 0.0279).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from laxative treatment.

claim: Lactulose increased microbiota density.
source: Of the laxatives, PEG 3350 reduced microbiota density (p = 2.22 x 10−4), while lactulose increased it (p = 0.0279).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from laxative treatment.

claim: The anti-motility agent loperamide had no significant effect on microbiota density.
source: The anti-motility agent loperamide and the proton pump inhibitor omeprazole had no significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant change in microbiota density with loperamide treatment.

claim: The proton pump inhibitor omeprazole had no significant effect on microbiota density.
source: The anti-motility agent loperamide and the proton pump inhibitor omeprazole had no significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant change in microbiota density with omeprazole treatment.

claim: Alpha diversity and microbiota density are significantly correlated across pharmacologic treatments.
source: Across the pharmacologics, we never observe high microbiota density with low alpha diversity, which drives a significant correlation between alpha diversity and microbiota density (ρ = 0.628, p < 0.0001, Spearman correlation; Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: High alpha diversity with low microbiota density is commonly observed in pharmacologic treatments.
source: However, we commonly observe high alpha diversity with low microbiota density (e.g., animals given metronidazole; Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), suggesting changes in microbiota density do not strictly correspond to changes in alpha diversity (see Supplemental Results and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from pharmacologic treatment data.

claim: Changes in microbiota density do not strictly correspond to changes in alpha diversity.
source: However, we commonly observe high alpha diversity with low microbiota density (e.g., animals given metronidazole; Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), suggesting changes in microbiota density do not strictly correspond to changes in alpha diversity (see Supplemental Results and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations showing dissociation between alpha diversity and microbiota density changes.

claim: There is no correlation between microbiota density and fecal water content across tested pharmacologics.
source: As with our results in the mammals, we found no correlation between microbiota density and fecal water content across the tested pharmacologics (ρ = -0.338, p = 0.411, Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between cecum size and microbiota density.
source: We found a significant negative correlation between cecum size and microbiota density (ρ = -0.729, p = 2.46 x 10−7, Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Epididymal fat pad mass is positively correlated with microbiota density.
source: Epididymal fat pad mass, fecal IgA, and lamina propria FoxP3+CD4+ regulatory T cells were each positively correlated with microbiota density (ρfat = 0.587, pfat = 6.11 x 10−5; ρIgA = 0.783, pIgA = 3.35 x 10−7; ρTreg = 0.639, pTreg = 5.31 x 10−6; Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Fecal IgA is positively correlated with microbiota density.
source: Epididymal fat pad mass, fecal IgA, and lamina propria FoxP3+CD4+ regulatory T cells were each positively correlated with microbiota density (ρfat = 0.587, pfat = 6.11 x 10−5; ρIgA = 0.783, pIgA = 3.35 x 10−7; ρTreg = 0.639, pTreg = 5.31 x 10−6; Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Lamina propria FoxP3+CD4+ regulatory T cells are positively correlated with microbiota density.
source: Epididymal fat pad mass, fecal IgA, and lamina propria FoxP3+CD4+ regulatory T cells were each positively correlated with microbiota density (ρfat = 0.587, pfat = 6.11 x 10−5; ρIgA = 0.783, pIgA = 3.35 x 10−7; ρTreg = 0.639, pTreg = 5.31 x 10−6; Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Subjects with IBD had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls.
source: Concordant with prior work using phylum-specific qPCR (Frank et al., 2007) and flow cytometry (CD-only; Vandeputte et al., 2017b), subjects with IBD had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls (pUC = 0.00181, pCD = 1.77×10−4, pIPAA = 2.40×10−5, each vs Healthy, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3A), even when excluding individuals receiving antibiotics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is concordant with prior published work using different methods.

claim: Subjects with ulcerative colitis had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls.
source: Concordant with prior work using phylum-specific qPCR (Frank et al., 2007) and flow cytometry (CD-only; Vandeputte et al., 2017b), subjects with IBD had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls (pUC = 0.00181, pCD = 1.77×10−4, pIPAA = 2.40×10−5, each vs Healthy, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3A), even when excluding individuals receiving antibiotics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing UC subjects to healthy controls.

claim: Subjects with Crohn's disease had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls.
source: Concordant with prior work using phylum-specific qPCR (Frank et al., 2007) and flow cytometry (CD-only; Vandeputte et al., 2017b), subjects with IBD had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls (pUC = 0.00181, pCD = 1.77×10−4, pIPAA = 2.40×10−5, each vs Healthy, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3A), even when excluding individuals receiving antibiotics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing CD subjects to healthy controls.

claim: IPAA subjects had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls.
source: Concordant with prior work using phylum-specific qPCR (Frank et al., 2007) and flow cytometry (CD-only; Vandeputte et al., 2017b), subjects with IBD had decreased microbiota density compared to healthy controls (pUC = 0.00181, pCD = 1.77×10−4, pIPAA = 2.40×10−5, each vs Healthy, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3A), even when excluding individuals receiving antibiotics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing IPAA subjects to healthy controls.

claim: Individuals with active CD had increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals.
source: Individuals with active CD, as well as IPAA subjects, had increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals (pactive CD = 0.036, pIPAA = 0.0184, each vs Healthy; Tukey's HSD), while individuals with UC or inactive CD did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing fecal water content.

claim: IPAA subjects had increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals.
source: Individuals with active CD, as well as IPAA subjects, had increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals (pactive CD = 0.036, pIPAA = 0.0184, each vs Healthy; Tukey's HSD), while individuals with UC or inactive CD did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing fecal water content.

claim: Individuals with UC did not have increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals.
source: Individuals with active CD, as well as IPAA subjects, had increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals (pactive CD = 0.036, pIPAA = 0.0184, each vs Healthy; Tukey's HSD), while individuals with UC or inactive CD did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in fecal water content.

claim: Individuals with inactive CD did not have increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals.
source: Individuals with active CD, as well as IPAA subjects, had increased fecal water content compared to healthy individuals (pactive CD = 0.036, pIPAA = 0.0184, each vs Healthy; Tukey's HSD), while individuals with UC or inactive CD did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in fecal water content.

claim: The decrease in microbiota density in IBD compared to healthy controls was consistent across individuals with active disease or inactive disease.
source: Nonetheless, the decrease in microbiota density in IBD compared to healthy controls was consistent across individuals with active disease or inactive disease (pactive IBD = 7.68 x 10−5, pactive CD = 0.000466, pinactive IBD = 0.00229, pinactive CD = 0.0479, each vs Healthy, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3B), demonstrating that the microbiota density changes in IBD were not simply driven by the increased fecal water content that occurred with active inflammation in CD.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data stratified by disease activity.

claim: The microbiota density changes in IBD were not simply driven by the increased fecal water content that occurred with active inflammation in CD.
source: Nonetheless, the decrease in microbiota density in IBD compared to healthy controls was consistent across individuals with active disease or inactive disease (pactive IBD = 7.68 x 10−5, pactive CD = 0.000466, pinactive IBD = 0.00229, pinactive CD = 0.0479, each vs Healthy, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3B), demonstrating that the microbiota density changes in IBD were not simply driven by the increased fecal water content that occurred with active inflammation in CD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that microbiota density is reduced in both active and inactive disease despite differences in water content.

claim: The IBD microbiome had a decreased alpha diversity compared to healthy subjects.
source: In line with previous studies (Frank et al., 2007; Gevers et al., 2014; Gophna et al., 2006; Jacobs et al., 2016), the IBD microbiome had a decreased alpha diversity compared to healthy subjects (pUC = 0.00339, pCD = 2.39×10−9, pIPAA = 1.17×10−12, each vs Healthy; Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is consistent with previous published studies.

claim: Decreases in gut microbiota density were most significantly correlated with decreases in Firmicutes.
source: When we multiplied each taxa's relative abundance by the microbiota density to calculate their absolute abundances, we found decreases in gut microbiota density were most significantly correlated with decreases in Firmicutes, while Proteobacteria were the only one of the four major phyla in the gut microbiota that were not correlated with microbiota density (Figure 3E–3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of absolute abundance data calculated from relative abundance and microbiota density.

claim: Proteobacteria were the only one of the four major phyla in the gut microbiota that were not correlated with microbiota density.
source: When we multiplied each taxa's relative abundance by the microbiota density to calculate their absolute abundances, we found decreases in gut microbiota density were most significantly correlated with decreases in Firmicutes, while Proteobacteria were the only one of the four major phyla in the gut microbiota that were not correlated with microbiota density (Figure 3E–3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship between Proteobacteria abundance and microbiota density.

claim: In absolute terms, Proteobacteria are able to sustain a constant density in individuals with IBD while the remaining phyla decrease in density.
source: These results from measuring the density of each phyla provide a novel insight compared to previous studies that associated a relative increase in the proportion of Proteobacteria with IBD (Frank et al., 2007; Gevers et al., 2014). We show here that in absolute terms, Proteobacteria are able to sustain a constant density in the individuals with IBD while the remaining phyla decrease in density.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of absolute abundance data showing constant Proteobacteria levels despite overall density reduction.

claim: The rCDI gut microbiota has a significantly lower microbiota density than the donor microbiota.
source: In fecal samples from FMT donors and their rCDI FMT recipients prior to and after FMT, we observed that the rCDI gut microbiota has a significantly lower microbiota density than the donor microbiota, and that FMT increased microbiota density (p < 0.05 for all comparisons, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing rCDI and donor samples.

claim: FMT increased microbiota density in rCDI recipients.
source: In fecal samples from FMT donors and their rCDI FMT recipients prior to and after FMT, we observed that the rCDI gut microbiota has a significantly lower microbiota density than the donor microbiota, and that FMT increased microbiota density (p < 0.05 for all comparisons, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing pre- and post-FMT samples.

claim: There were no differences in fecal water content between the donors and recipients before or after FMT.
source: We did not observe any differences in fecal water content between the donors and recipients before or after FMT (p > 0.2 for all comparisons, Tukey's HSD).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant differences in fecal water content.

claim: rCDI FMT recipients had both a relative and absolute increase in Proteobacteria that was significantly reduced by FMT.
source: In addition, we found that rCDI FMT recipients had both a relative and absolute increase in Proteobacteria that was significantly reduced by FMT (Figure 4B and C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data showing changes in Proteobacteria abundance.

claim: FMT restores higher densities of Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria to more fully realize the host's carrying capacity.
source: These data suggest that FMT restores higher densities of Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria to more fully realize the host's carrying capacity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that FMT increases microbiota density by restoring specific phyla.

claim: The microbiota density of mice colonized with healthy samples was greater than that of mice colonized with rCDI samples.
source: The microbiota density of mice colonized with the healthy samples (a) was greater than that of mice colonized with rCDI samples (b) (p = 1.79×10−4, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4E), suggesting that rCDI individuals have a reduced microbiota fitness compared to healthy donors.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from gnotobiotic mouse experiments.

claim: rCDI individuals have a reduced microbiota fitness compared to healthy donors.
source: The microbiota density of mice colonized with the healthy samples (a) was greater than that of mice colonized with rCDI samples (b) (p = 1.79×10−4, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4E), suggesting that rCDI individuals have a reduced microbiota fitness compared to healthy donors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that rCDI microbiotas reach lower densities in a controlled mouse environment.

claim: Following the introduction of the healthy donor microbiota to the mice colonized with the rCDI microbiota, microbiota density increased.
source: Following the introduction of the healthy donor microbiota to the mice colonized with the rCDI microbiota (c), we observed increased microbiota density in these mice (p = 6.88×10−8, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4E), implying a restoration of microbiota fitness.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the mouse FMT model.

claim: The introduction of healthy donor microbiota to mice colonized with rCDI microbiota implies a restoration of microbiota fitness.
source: Following the introduction of the healthy donor microbiota to the mice colonized with the rCDI microbiota (c), we observed increased microbiota density in these mice (p = 6.88×10−8, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4E), implying a restoration of microbiota fitness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that adding healthy donor microbiota increases density in mice with rCDI microbiota.

claim: When germ-free mice are colonized with the microbiota of individuals with rCDI 6-12 months after they received an FMT, their microbiota fitness had been restored.
source: Furthermore, when we colonize germ-free mice with the microbiota of the individuals with rCDI 6–12 months after they received an FMT (d), we find that their microbiota fitness had been restored, just as in our mouse FMT model (p = 8.60×10−8, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, followed by a Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from gnotobiotic mice colonized with post-FMT samples.

claim: FMT successfully treats the fitness defect of the rCDI community.
source: These findings in the mice model recapitulate the data in our human cohort of FMT recipients and suggest that FMT successfully treats the fitness defect of the rCDI community.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations in human and mouse FMT experiments showing restoration of microbiota fitness.

claim: The DNA-based microbiota density estimation method can be incorporated into existing 16S rRNA and metagenomic workflows by simply weighing the input sample.
source: The DNA-based microbiota density estimation method employed here and in previous studies (Faith et al., 2011; Llewellyn et al., 2018; Reyes et al., 2013) has the advantage that it can be incorporated into existing 16S rRNA and metagenomic workflows by simply weighing the input sample and ensuring the input mass of fecal material is within the linear range of the DNA extraction protocol.
evidence: The claim is supported by methodological description and references to previous studies using this approach.

claim: A very significant correlation exists between the viability-based CFU density measurement and the DNA-based density measurement.
source: However, in practice we found that the influence of any variation from live/dead bacteria was sufficiently low that it did not influence the major conclusions of this study; we observed a very significant correlation between the viability-based CFU density measurement and the DNA-based one and all of the major relationships observed in this study were consistent across both approaches (i.e., variation across mammals, IBD and IPAA lower density than healthy, rCDI lower density than FMT donor or rCDI post-transplant; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis comparing CFU and DNA-based density measurements.

claim: All of the major relationships observed in this study were consistent across both CFU-based and DNA-based density approaches.
source: However, in practice we found that the influence of any variation from live/dead bacteria was sufficiently low that it did not influence the major conclusions of this study; we observed a very significant correlation between the viability-based CFU density measurement and the DNA-based one and all of the major relationships observed in this study were consistent across both approaches (i.e., variation across mammals, IBD and IPAA lower density than healthy, rCDI lower density than FMT donor or rCDI post-transplant; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of results obtained using both measurement methods.

claim: Microbiota density and fecal water content can both be altered by pharmacologics.
source: While both microbiota density and fecal water content vary across mammals and can be altered by pharmacologics (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), dietary components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Llewellyn et al., 2018), and host disease status (Figures 3 and 4), we find microbiota density is consistently not correlated with water content.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of pharmacologics on both parameters.

claim: Microbiota density and fecal water content can both be altered by dietary components.
source: While both microbiota density and fecal water content vary across mammals and can be altered by pharmacologics (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), dietary components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Llewellyn et al., 2018), and host disease status (Figures 3 and 4), we find microbiota density is consistently not correlated with water content.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work showing dietary effects.

claim: Microbiota density and fecal water content can both be altered by host disease status.
source: While both microbiota density and fecal water content vary across mammals and can be altered by pharmacologics (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), dietary components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Llewellyn et al., 2018), and host disease status (Figures 3 and 4), we find microbiota density is consistently not correlated with water content.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from disease cohorts showing changes in both parameters.

claim: Microbiota density is consistently not correlated with water content.
source: While both microbiota density and fecal water content vary across mammals and can be altered by pharmacologics (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), dietary components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Llewellyn et al., 2018), and host disease status (Figures 3 and 4), we find microbiota density is consistently not correlated with water content.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analyses across multiple experimental conditions showing no significant relationship.

claim: The best predictor of the impact of changes of microbiota density on host physiology was when density was calculated with stool wet weight.
source: In the context of altering host physiology through antibiotic manipulation of microbiota density, the best predictor of the impact of changes of microbiota density on host physiology was when density was calculated with stool wet weight, suggesting both wet and dry components of stool are important diluents in determining microbiota density and its impact on the host.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of wet weight versus dry weight as predictors in linear models of host physiology.

claim: Both wet and dry components of stool are important diluents in determining microbiota density and its impact on the host.
source: In the context of altering host physiology through antibiotic manipulation of microbiota density, the best predictor of the impact of changes of microbiota density on host physiology was when density was calculated with stool wet weight, suggesting both wet and dry components of stool are important diluents in determining microbiota density and its impact on the host.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that wet weight is a better predictor than dry weight for host physiology outcomes.

claim: Microbiota density may change independently of water content.
source: Our results suggest that microbiota density may change independently of water content, implying that the density of microbes can be altered independently of water and other contents of the stool bulk, such as undigested dietary components or host tissue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of correlation between microbiota density and water content across conditions.

claim: The density of microbes can be altered independently of water and other contents of the stool bulk.
source: Our results suggest that microbiota density may change independently of water content, implying that the density of microbes can be altered independently of water and other contents of the stool bulk, such as undigested dietary components or host tissue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations showing microbiota density changes without corresponding water content changes.

claim: Differences in microbiota density can be influenced by both the host's carrying capacity and the fitness of the microbiota to reach the carrying capacity of a given host.
source: Differences in microbiota density can be influenced by both the host's carrying capacity and the fitness of the microbiota to reach the carrying capacity of a given host.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of mammalian surveys and gnotobiotic experiments.

claim: The density of gut microbes varies across mammals and is more similar in more phylogenetically related species.
source: We found the density of gut microbes varies across mammals and is more similar in more phylogenetically related species.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing density differences at the order level.

claim: Gut architecture appears to be a major driver of microbiota density across mammals.
source: Across mammals, gut architecture appears to be a major driver of density, as the lowest densities were observed in order Carnivora, whose short, simple intestines have a lower carrying capacity and are maladapted for microbial fermentation at high densities.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Carnivora with simple gut architectures have the lowest densities.

claim: The lowest microbiota densities were observed in order Carnivora, whose short, simple intestines have a lower carrying capacity and are maladapted for microbial fermentation at high densities.
source: Across mammals, gut architecture appears to be a major driver of density, as the lowest densities were observed in order Carnivora, whose short, simple intestines have a lower carrying capacity and are maladapted for microbial fermentation at high densities.
evidence: The claim combines experimental data on density with established knowledge about Carnivora gut anatomy.

claim: The low microbiota density of the red panda supports intestinal architecture as a major determinant of host carrying capacity.
source: The low microbiota density of the red panda, a member of Carnivora with a herbivorous diet, further supports intestinal architecture as a major determinant of host carrying capacity and thus a driver of microbiota density.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that red panda has low density despite herbivorous diet, suggesting anatomy is key.

claim: The significantly reduced microbiota density in humans with IPAA demonstrates that changing gut architecture within a species is capable of influencing host carrying capacity.
source: Finally, the significantly reduced microbiota density in humans with IPAA uniquely demonstrates that changing gut architecture within a species (in this case by surgery to treat ulcerative colitis) is equally capable of influencing host carrying capacity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that surgical alteration of gut architecture in IPAA patients reduces microbiota density.

claim: Microbiota density can be altered with pharmacologics within a murine host with controlled carrying capacity.
source: Within a murine host with controlled carrying capacity (i.e., fixed diet, genetics, housing, etc.), we found microbiota density can be altered with pharmacologics, with downstream consequences to host adiposity and immune function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacologic treatment experiments in mice.

claim: Altering microbiota density with pharmacologics has downstream consequences to host adiposity and immune function.
source: Within a murine host with controlled carrying capacity (i.e., fixed diet, genetics, housing, etc.), we found microbiota density can be altered with pharmacologics, with downstream consequences to host adiposity and immune function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlations between microbiota density and host phenotypes.

claim: Different antibiotics were highly varied in their ability to impact microbiota density.
source: Different antibiotics were highly varied in their ability to impact microbiota density, which could explain the mixed efficacy of antibiotics in microbiota-targeted clinical trials for complex disease and varied responses to antibiotics in animal models.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of antibiotics on microbiota density.

claim: The varied ability of antibiotics to impact microbiota density could explain the mixed efficacy of antibiotics in microbiota-targeted clinical trials for complex disease.
source: Different antibiotics were highly varied in their ability to impact microbiota density, which could explain the mixed efficacy of antibiotics in microbiota-targeted clinical trials for complex disease and varied responses to antibiotics in animal models.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential explanation for clinical trial outcomes based on the observed variation in antibiotic effects.

claim: Identifying more effective microbiota depleting cocktails would improve the design of microbiota-targeted studies.
source: Identifying more effective microbiota depleting cocktails would improve the design of such studies, while measuring microbiota density in trials with antibiotics could better stratify clinical response.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential improvements to study design based on the findings.

claim: Measuring microbiota density in trials with antibiotics could better stratify clinical response.
source: Identifying more effective microbiota depleting cocktails would improve the design of such studies, while measuring microbiota density in trials with antibiotics could better stratify clinical response.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential application of microbiota density measurements in clinical trials.

claim: Microbiota density can be manipulated by dietary changes.
source: Previous studies have observed that microbiota density can be manipulated by dietary changes (Llewellyn et al., 2018; Sonnenburg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous published studies.

claim: Altering microbiota density with either diet or antibiotics could modify colitis severity.
source: Furthermore, we found that altering microbiota density with either diet or antibiotics could modify colitis severity (Llewellyn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Chronically low microbiota density may play a role in the development or progression of IBD.
source: Coupled with our findings that changes in microbiota density can alter host metabolism and immune populations, these results suggest that chronically low microbiota density may play a role in the development or progression of disease.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential role for low microbiota density in disease based on the observed associations.

claim: An initial reduction in microbiota density might contribute to a pro-inflammatory host immune system that creates a positive feedback loop that sustains a low microbiota density.
source: It might even be possible that an initial reduction in microbiota density contributes to a pro-inflammatory host immune system that creates a positive feedback loop that sustains a low microbiota density.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanistic explanation for sustained low density in disease.

claim: A low microbiota density, if due to low microbiota fitness, may have reduced colonization resistance, allowing for pathogens or pathobionts to take hold and contribute to disease processes.
source: It is also possible that a low microbiota density, if due to low microbiota fitness, has reduced colonization resistance, allowing for pathogens or pathobionts to take hold and contribute to disease processes in the host (Battaglioli et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism linking low density to disease, with support from a cited study.

claim: The reduced microbiota density in rCDI is due to a lack of microbiota fitness.
source: Finally, we found that the reduced microbiota density in rCDI, due to a lack of microbiota fitness, was 'druggable' by FMT.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from gnotobiotic mouse experiments showing rCDI microbiota has reduced fitness.

claim: The reduced microbiota density in rCDI was 'druggable' by FMT.
source: Finally, we found that the reduced microbiota density in rCDI, due to a lack of microbiota fitness, was 'druggable' by FMT.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing FMT increases microbiota density in rCDI.

claim: Studying the factors that determine both host carrying capacity and microbiota fitness may allow prediction of which disease states may benefit from therapeutics that target the host versus ones that target the microbiota.
source: Moving forward, studying the factors that determine both host carrying capacity and microbiota fitness may allow us to predict which disease states may benefit from therapeutics that target the host versus ones that target the microbiota.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential future applications of understanding carrying capacity and fitness.

claim: Exploring how FMT is able to increase microbiota fitness and therefore microbiota density should provide mechanistic insights into FMT for rCDI that can be used for other potential indications for FMT.
source: For example, exploring how FMT is able to increase microbiota fitness and therefore microbiota density should provide mechanistic insights into FMT for rCDI that can be used for other potential indications for FMT.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential future research directions and applications.

claim: Routine monitoring could identify individuals with microbiota fitness deficiencies that might benefit from prophylactic microbial therapeutics to boost colonization resistance to treat or prevent disease.
source: These results also suggest that routine monitoring could identify individuals with microbiota fitness deficiencies that might benefit from prophylactic microbial therapeutics to boost colonization resistance to treat or prevent disease (Battaglioli et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential clinical application of microbiota density monitoring.

claim: Fecal microbial DNA content correlates with flow cytometry counts and colony-forming units (CFU).
source: Here, we use fecal microbial DNA content to estimate gut microbiota density, since it correlates with flow cytometry counts and colony-forming units (CFU), and it can be easily incorporated into standard microbiome sequencing workflows by weighing the sample (Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study demonstrating this correlation.

claim: Fecal microbial DNA content can be easily incorporated into standard microbiome sequencing workflows by weighing the sample.
source: Here, we use fecal microbial DNA content to estimate gut microbiota density, since it correlates with flow cytometry counts and colony-forming units (CFU), and it can be easily incorporated into standard microbiome sequencing workflows by weighing the sample (Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by methodological description and citation to previous work.

claim: The microbiome's influence on host physiology likely depends on the number – and not just the type – of bacteria interfacing with the host.
source: The microbiome's influence on host physiology likely depends on the number – and not just the type – of bacteria interfacing with the host.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the importance of absolute bacterial numbers in host-microbe interactions.

claim: Understanding factors driving gut microbiota density may advance the therapeutic potential of the microbiota.
source: Therefore, understanding factors driving gut microbiota density, as well as the impact of microbiota density on health, may advance the therapeutic potential of the microbiota.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential benefits of understanding microbiota density.

claim: Understanding the impact of microbiota density on health may advance the therapeutic potential of the microbiota.
source: Therefore, understanding factors driving gut microbiota density, as well as the impact of microbiota density on health, may advance the therapeutic potential of the microbiota.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential benefits of understanding microbiota density's health impacts.

claim: Polymyxin B did not reduce the microbiota density overall.
source: Polymyxin B did not reduce the microbiota density overall, and did not significantly reduce the absolute abundance of Gram-negative bacteria (p = 0.116, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or change the absolute abundance of Gram-positive bacteria (p = 0.273, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Polymyxin B did not significantly reduce the absolute abundance of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Polymyxin B did not reduce the microbiota density overall, and did not significantly reduce the absolute abundance of Gram-negative bacteria (p = 0.116, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or change the absolute abundance of Gram-positive bacteria (p = 0.273, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: Polymyxin B did not change the absolute abundance of Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Polymyxin B did not reduce the microbiota density overall, and did not significantly reduce the absolute abundance of Gram-negative bacteria (p = 0.116, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or change the absolute abundance of Gram-positive bacteria (p = 0.273, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: Vancomycin drove a significant decrease in the absolute abundance of both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms.
source: Vancomycin, on the other hand, drove a significant decrease in the absolute abundance of both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms (pGram(+) = 6.27×10−13, pGram(-) = 6.27×10−13, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: The spectrum of activity of antibiotics as determined by in vitro assays may not reflect the effects of these drugs in vivo when introduced to complex communities of organisms.
source: These results suggest that the spectrum of activity of antibiotics as determined by in vitro assays may not reflect the effects of these drugs in vivo, when they are introduced to complex communities of organisms such as in the gut.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that antibiotic effects in vivo differ from their expected spectrum based on in vitro activity.

claim: Low dose vancomycin led to a relative expansion of Verrucomicrobia and Firmicutes.
source: We found that vancomycin exerted selective pressure against susceptible organisms leading to a relative expansion of Verrucomicrobia and Firmicutes in the low and high dose groups respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B ).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data showing changes in relative abundance.

claim: High dose vancomycin led to a relative expansion of Firmicutes.
source: We found that vancomycin exerted selective pressure against susceptible organisms leading to a relative expansion of Verrucomicrobia and Firmicutes in the low and high dose groups respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B ).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data showing changes in relative abundance.

claim: Low dose vancomycin caused a bloom of Verrucomicrobia in absolute terms.
source: When we multiplied each taxa's relative abundance by the microbiota density to calculate their absolute abundances, we observed a bloom of Verrucomicrobia in the low dose group (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C ).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of absolute abundance data calculated from relative abundance and microbiota density.

claim: High dose vancomycin successfully depleted members of all phyla, including Firmicutes.
source: Surprisingly, in the high dose group, we found that vancomycin successfully depleted members of all phyla, including Firmicutes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D ).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of absolute abundance data showing depletion across all phyla.

claim: Microbiota density and alpha diversity were not significantly correlated in vancomycin treatment experiments.
source: Microbiota density and alpha diversity were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.107; p = 0.557; Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), as both low dose and high dose vancomycin significantly reduced alpha diversity (plow = 6.10 x 10−5 and phigh = 0.00223, final timepoint vs baseline, Mann Whitney; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F ), while only high dose vancomycin reduced microbiota density (plow = 0.669, phigh = 0.0127, final timepoint vs baseline, Mann Whitney; Figure 2—figure supplement 2G ).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: Both low dose and high dose vancomycin significantly reduced alpha diversity.
source: Microbiota density and alpha diversity were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.107; p = 0.557; Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), as both low dose and high dose vancomycin significantly reduced alpha diversity (plow = 6.10 x 10−5 and phigh = 0.00223, final timepoint vs baseline, Mann Whitney; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F ), while only high dose vancomycin reduced microbiota density (plow = 0.669, phigh = 0.0127, final timepoint vs baseline, Mann Whitney; Figure 2—figure supplement 2G ).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing baseline and final timepoint alpha diversity.

claim: Only high dose vancomycin reduced microbiota density.
source: Microbiota density and alpha diversity were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.107; p = 0.557; Spearman; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), as both low dose and high dose vancomycin significantly reduced alpha diversity (plow = 6.10 x 10−5 and phigh = 0.00223, final timepoint vs baseline, Mann Whitney; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F ), while only high dose vancomycin reduced microbiota density (plow = 0.669, phigh = 0.0127, final timepoint vs baseline, Mann Whitney; Figure 2—figure supplement 2G ).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing baseline and final timepoint microbiota density.

claim: Fungal reads accounted for only 0.112% of mapped reads in one rCDI sample.
source: Using this approach, we were only able to identify fungal reads in one of the eighteen samples. In this sample, Saccharomyces cerevisiae was the only identified fungi and comprised 0.112% of the mapped reads, while the remaining 99.9% were mapped to bacteria, consistent with previous reports of fungal reads accounting for approximately 0.1% of the human gut metagenome (MetaHIT Consortium et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by metagenomic sequencing data analysis.

claim: Fungal reads account for approximately 0.1% of the human gut metagenome.
source: Using this approach, we were only able to identify fungal reads in one of the eighteen samples. In this sample, Saccharomyces cerevisiae was the only identified fungi and comprised 0.112% of the mapped reads, while the remaining 99.9% were mapped to bacteria, consistent with previous reports of fungal reads accounting for approximately 0.1% of the human gut metagenome (MetaHIT Consortium et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The phenol:chloroform extraction method is capable of isolating fungal DNA.
source: Furthermore, the identification of fungal reads in our samples demonstrates our methods were capable of isolating at least a proportion of the fungal DNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the detection of fungal reads in samples processed with this method.
